Democrats Trade Blame Over Battleground Senate Races as Election Day Nears
 
Plus, the U.S. pushes to restore Russian gas sales to Europe via Ukraine, and how an elite liberal-arts school became the best college bargain
 
 
EMILY ROSE BENNETT FOR WSJ
 

1. FROM MY DESK

 

Democrats have a chance to retake the Senate—a proposition that seemed far-fetched earlier this year. But instead of unity ahead of Election Day, our reporting shows infighting and finger-pointing are already under way. 

 

Allies of the party’s leaders privately say that an insurgent left wing has unnecessarily sucked time and money into races that should have been easier for Democrats, to the detriment of other candidates. Progressives say the party’s establishment isn’t doing everything possible to help them win.

 

Both factions want a Democratic Senate, and winning may soothe the acrimony. But whatever the outcome, Tuesday’s results are poised to accelerate an internecine battle for the future of the party. Follow our live coverage for real-time updates, analysis and news as the midterms unfold.

 

This is an edition of The 10-Point newsletter, a guided tour of the best coverage in The Wall Street Journal. If you’re not subscribed, sign up here. If you’re reading this in your inbox, tap the headline above for online and audio versions of this newsletter.

 
 
 

2. TODAY’S HEADLINES

 

• Rep. Haley Stevens stunned Democrats less than 48 hours before Election Day by endorsing Republican Mike Rogers over her former primary opponent, Abdul El-Sayed. Stevens’s journey from team player to pariah showcases some of the Democratic Party’s deepest divisions and the potential for politics to deliver the unexpected.

 

• A business jet crashed in Florida, killing all nine people on board.

 

• Virginia and other states are trying to slow “super speeders” with GPS technology that prevents their cars from blowing the speed limit.

 

• Stretched public finances and a rapidly aging population are threatening Europe’s great pension covenant, stoking fear and anger over the future of a cradle-to-grave welfare state voters had long taken for granted.

 

• Miami’s luxurious Design District is designated an Opportunity Zone under a nearly decade-old federal provision created to encourage investment in lower-income communities by offering tax breaks.

• Netflix’s growth increasingly hinges on advertising, which depends heavily on how much people watch—and lately, they haven’t been watching as much. That makes Netflix look less like a growth stock and more like a company waiting for its next hit, writes David Wainer.

 
 
 

4. READ IT HERE FIRST

 

The U.S. is pushing to restore Russian gas sales to Europe via Ukraine.

 

The U.S. is backing a quick resumption of Russian natural-gas sales to Europe via pipelines running through Moscow’s wartime enemy—Ukraine—as part of negotiations aimed at securing an energy ceasefire ahead of the coming winter, according to U.S., European and Ukrainian officials. The idea, broached by U.S. envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff during trips to Moscow and Kyiv in September, would involve selling Russian gas via a U.S. intermediary to circumvent European sanctions—and could create a lucrative opportunity for U.S. investors, people who attended the discussions said. But the idea faces resistance in European capitals, report Yaroslav Trofimov, Drew Hinshaw and Joe Parkinson.

 

5.

 

The U.S. once dominated the world’s oceans. China’s Xi is changing that.

 

For centuries, China was a continental force. Today, the country is undertaking one of the largest peacetime naval buildups in modern history. Its sudden, historic emergence as one of the world’s top maritime powers is challenging the U.S. on a scale it hasn’t faced since World War II, report Niharika Mandhana, Josh Chin and Camille Bressange. The transformation is driven in part by Chinese leader Xi Jinping’s conviction that the rise and fall of nations is linked inextricably to the oceans. On any given day, as many as 100 of China’s navy ships are out on some of Asia’s busiest trade and transportation routes—pressuring rivals and training for a potential conflict with the U.S.

6. SEE THE STORY

 

The best college bargain is a super-pricey elite liberal arts school.

 
 
 

Students at Williams College pay less to attend on average than the in-state cost at the University of Massachusetts Amherst. Those at Grinnell College pay less than Iowans going to the University of Iowa. And at Swarthmore College, the average student pays roughly half of what peers fork out at Penn State. A growing group of elite liberal-arts colleges long known for eye-watering price tags is turning out to be quite the bargain for many students—and the schools want you to know it.

8. THE NUMBER

 
13 seconds
 

The razor-thin margin separating Sweden’s Andreas Almgren from Italian runner-up Yemaneberhan Crippa at the New York City Marathon. Almgren, 31, who had never run a competitive marathon before this race, pulled away from Crippa in the final mile to win in 2:06:01—the third-fastest time in the course’s history. He was the first-ever NYC winner from Sweden. Kenya’s Sheila Chepkirui won the women’s race for the second time, repeating her 2024 victory.

 
 
 

9. AND FINALLY…

 

Companies have a solution for the skilled trade shortage: more women.

 

The skilled trades have long been a boy’s club. But more women are breaking in, drawn by well-paying jobs that are in high demand. To keep them coming, many companies are courting women through new benefits and perks, including paid maternity leave and more flexibility. They are also trying to create a more welcoming work environment while cracking down on off-color jokes and catcalls on male-dominated jobsites.
